items.title: Infosys walked away from 25% of its revenue | Narayana Murthy #shorts
items.caption:
Infosys founder NR Narayana Murthy on the toughest decision of his life.

In 1995, Infosys had just gone public. He decided not to renew the contract with a Fortune 10 company that made up 25% of its revenue. The other top players in the field all signed on the dotted line, and his younger colleagues were not in favour. "I was the only crazy guy."

Would you have walked away from 25% of your revenue?

Source: moneycontrol Startup Conclave, NR Narayana Murthy in conversation with Rohan Murty (@moneycontrol). Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=kHgsOppb1WM

items.title: Why Narayana Murthy didn't keep most of Infosys #shorts
items.caption:
Rohan Murty asked his father why he chose not to keep as much of the company at its inception as modern founders do.

NR Narayana Murthy: "I enjoyed the company of people who thought that it was their company." He knew he couldn't keep the major percentage and expect others to give their all. "These are all personal philosophies."

Would you give away equity to build a team that feels like owners?

items.title: Narayana Murthy: smarter classmates didn't have the luck #shorts
items.caption:
Destiny or luck for an entrepreneur? Infosys founder NR Narayana Murthy's answer.

When logic couldn't give him an answer, faith gave him strength. Quoting "When God is shy to announce His presence, He comes in the form of chance," he says many classmates were smarter than him but didn't have the luck to be where he was, and believing in luck brings humility.

Do you believe in luck or only hard work?

items.title: He resigned on his wife's birthday | Narayana Murthy #shorts
items.caption:
NR Narayana Murthy on the support that made Infosys possible.

He resigned on his wife's birthday, 19 August 1976. When he told her, she smiled and said: "Not an issue. We will live within whatever means we have. I will fully support you and you will succeed."

Who backed you when you took your biggest risk?

items.title: Money only prolongs failure | Anant Goel, Milkbasket #shorts
items.caption:
Can funding save a bad business model? Milkbasket co-founder Anant Goel says no.

Now building Handpickd, he says commerce is not a space where money changes the outcome: "Money can prolong the failure outcome." A customer cannot get the best quality at the cheapest price in the fastest time, so every business model needs a compromise. Without one, it is too good to be true and it will fail.

What compromise does your business make?

items.title: 10-minute delivery, 3 months on the road | Anant Goel #shorts
items.caption:
Your 10-minute order may have spent 3 months on the road.

Anant Goel, who co-founded Milkbasket and now runs Handpickd, says we should stop worrying only about how fast an order arrives and ask how long the product took to reach us. "Can those three months be reduced to eight hours?" His view: freshness matters when food matters.

Would you wait until tomorrow morning for fresher food?

items.title: People in Camellias want MORE discount | Anant Goel #shorts
items.caption:
Are wealthy customers really willing to pay a premium? Anant Goel does not think so.

The Milkbasket co-founder and Handpickd founder says people in Camellias want more discount than people outside it. His example: "if our salon charges us only 500 rupees for a haircut, then why am I paying 900 for that?" On the idea that people will pay a premium: "Somehow I don't believe that."

Do richer customers bargain more? What have you seen?

items.title: CVs only get you a meeting | Anant Goel, Milkbasket #shorts
items.caption:
What does a repeat founder look for when hiring?

Anant Goel, Milkbasket co-founder and now building Handpickd, says a CV only decides whether he meets you. After that: "You hire for attitude. Experience can be taught." Basic attitude and basic analytical skills should be there, and the rest can be figured out together.

Would you hire on attitude over experience?

items.title: Most categories have room for only 2 brands | Shalabh Gupta, Nuuk #shorts
items.caption:
Can you name a third cola brand?

Shalabh Gupta, co-founder of the home appliance brand Nuuk, says customers build a ladder of brands in their heads. Coke and Pepsi. Maaza and Slice. "You can have infinite ladders, but most of those ladders have only two rungs on them." The first rung gets the lion's share, the second is a distant second. "There is no third."

Which category in India still has an empty first rung?

items.title: Make money off the first purchase | Shalabh Gupta, Nuuk #shorts
items.caption:
Should your P&L depend on customers coming back?

Nuuk co-founder Shalabh Gupta is not a big believer in relying on LTV versus CAC. His simple math: "make money off the first purchase" and don't depend on the customer returning. Plan for repeats and advertise to those customers, but even that is still marketing spend. Nuuk had a healthy contribution margin even in its first months, with only two or three products.

Does your business make money on the first order?

items.title: Founder instinct is not a bottomless reservoir | Shalabh Gupta, Nuuk #shorts
items.caption:
Scratching your own itch works once. What about the second product?

Shalabh Gupta, co-founder of Nuuk, says a lot of consumer startups are built on founder's instinct, but "that instinct is not a bottomless reservoir of insight." Your second or third instinct might be wrong. So Nuuk has a dedicated consumer insights team that reports to the founder, not to anyone incentivized to get it done fast.

How do you decide what to build next?

items.title: Missionaries vs mercenaries: who to hire | Shalabh Gupta, Nuuk #shorts
items.caption:
Who stays when things get hard?

Shalabh Gupta, co-founder of Nuuk, says bigger companies start attracting mercenary talent. Mercenaries are great at their job, "but they don't stay when the going gets tough." Missionaries are great too, and you get the time and opportunity to develop them. It is a framework he and co-founder Gazal Kalra use for a lot of their hiring today.

Have you worked with more missionaries or mercenaries?

items.title: What a Hans Zimmer concert taught a ₹20,000 crore founder | Vasant Sridhar, OfBusiness #shorts
items.caption:
India's manufacturers aren't the bottleneck. The missing piece is someone to conduct them.

Vasant Sridhar, co-founder of OfBusiness, watched Hans Zimmer play in Abu Dhabi and saw the same pattern as India's small manufacturers: cello, piano, drums, all brilliant, but "it's the orchestration layer that makes it fabulous." Rajkot has engineering, Tiruppur has knits and dyeing, Kanpur has tanneries. His view: "I don't think manufacturing or SME capability is a bottleneck."

Which Indian industry cluster do you think is most underrated?

items.title: Hire for slope, not intercept | Vasant Sridhar, OfBusiness #shorts
items.caption:
Stop hiring for experience. Hire for slope.

Vasant Sridhar, co-founder of OfBusiness, says what matters in hiring and team building "is not the intercept at hiring, but it's the slope." Experience is where someone starts. OfBusiness optimizes for great learners who can compound along with the company, and he says this is how a lot of great organizations are built.

Would you pick the experienced hire or the fast learner?

items.title: Hands off does not mean eyes off | Vasant Sridhar, OfBusiness #shorts
items.caption:
"Hands-off does not mean eyes-off or ears-off."

Vasant Sridhar, co-founder of OfBusiness, on how he changed as the company grew. He says he is slightly hands-off today, but still knows the production at one of his processing units in Manesar, and which grade didn't get produced. Decisions stay with a great team, and he steps in only if a problem comes to him as an escalation.

Have you worked with a boss who got this balance right?

items.title: You earn smart work through hard work | Vasant Sridhar, OfBusiness #shorts
items.caption:
Smart work is what hard work turns into.

Vasant Sridhar, co-founder of OfBusiness, says one needs to work extremely hard to learn how to work smart. He was working north of 12 hours at ITC out of interest and a sense of ownership. He says the leverage, maturity and better judgment kick in after that, and calls it a personal call, but it's okay in your 20s to work hard.

Do you agree, or is this outdated advice in your 20s?

items.title: Why FirstClub launched with no search button | Ayyappan Rajagopal #shorts
items.caption:
A shopping app with no search button. On purpose.

Ayyappan Rajagopal, co-founder and CEO of FirstClub, says average browsing time on their app is 12 minutes plus, against sub five minutes on any other shopping app he compares it with. On day one they did not even have search, so consumers would spend more time and add more to the basket. The catch: "the responsibility is on you to give right selection rather than an unending aisle."

Would you use a grocery app with no search?

items.title: When an unhappy customer says "I so want you to succeed" | Ayyappan Rajagopal #shorts
items.caption:
What a good customer complaint sounds like.

Ayyappan Rajagopal, co-founder and CEO of FirstClub, says every platform makes mistakes, and on most platforms the feedback is anger. At FirstClub, he says, 9 out of 10 times it sounds like this: the lady's finger you sent was not good, "I so want you guys to succeed," can you please fix it? To him, that is what going deeper with customers means.

Which brand would you complain to like this?

items.title: No top 10 FMCG brands at launch. Now they all want in | Ayyappan Rajagopal #shorts
items.caption:
FirstClub built a grocery business without India's top 10 companies.

Ayyappan Rajagopal, co-founder and CEO of FirstClub, says that if you sort the Sensex by market cap, they were not able to work with any of the top 10 companies. Now, he says, every single brand out of those 10 wants to come and build products for them. His takeaway: be sharp about your target customer, and treat it as market creation, not a market share game.

Is market creation harder than fighting for market share?

items.title: A ₹100 book gets tracked. A $100,000 payment doesn't | Anand Balaji, Xflow #shorts
items.caption:
A ₹100 book gets more updates than a $100,000 payment.

Anand Balaji, co-founder and CEO of Xflow, shares what a potential customer told him before Xflow started: a ₹100 book on Amazon or Flipkart sends six or seven notifications and a tracking URL. But once a customer says they have paid a $100,000 invoice, there is no clue where the money is, and neither side's bank knows. That, he says, is why cross-border B2B payments are stuck in the '90s.

Have you ever had to chase an international payment like this?

items.title: Can you call your investor at 2 AM? | Anand Balaji, Xflow #shorts
items.caption:
One question to ask before you take an investor's money.

Anand Balaji, co-founder and CEO of Xflow, says it's okay to give up sometimes on valuation, because an investor is almost like your spouse. The advice he got from one founder: will you be able to call this person at 2 AM when you have a problem? If not, a big brand name or a higher valuation doesn't make them right. Xflow had multiple offers in its seed round and did not go for the highest.

Would you take a lower valuation for the right investor?

items.title: The feature he'd launch before the product | Anand Balaji, Xflow #shorts
items.caption:
He would launch this one feature before the product.

Anand Balaji, co-founder and CEO of Xflow, says customers knew they were getting fleeced but not by how much. So Xflow started telling people: don't use us, just go to the website and know your cost first. Even non-customers began uploading their costs, and it became a strong inbound channel. His lesson: don't assume anything about the customer. "Know your cost" would have been his first launch.

What free tool could your startup launch before its product?

items.title: No answer to "where do you see yourself in 5 years"? | Anand Balaji, Xflow #shorts
items.caption:
You may not need an answer to the five-year question.

Anand Balaji, co-founder and CEO of Xflow, says he would never have had a great answer to that interview question, and he doesn't think you need one. If you are clear on your path, that's great, and he knows people who have succeeded that way. But there is an alternate path: do a bunch of different interesting things in your career and you probably arrive at it, which he feels is where he landed with Xflow.

Do you have a five-year plan, or are you following interesting problems?
